newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. military presence in Guam a boon to rescue.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military presence in Guam a boon to rescue.

text.p: The tragedy of the crash of a Korean Air Lines Co jumbo jet in Guam had one bright spot: With a heavy U.S. military presence, the island has a rescue force few other resort areas can match.
In a massive rescue operation, U.S. Naval and Air Force personnel quickly arrived on the scene of the accident in a remote jungle valley about 45 km (30 miles) from Andersen Air Force Base.

About 200 of the passengers on the flight from Seoul died when the plane slammed into the ground en route to Guam's main international airport. Officials at Korean Air Lines said about 30 passengers, mostly honeymooners, had been rescued.
An official from the air base said U.S. forces conduct accident response exercises on a year-round basis and were well-prepared for the rescue operation.
The military also works with local authorities in emergency response drills and concluded a recent round of drills in April.
"We train constantly for any type of contingency including disaster response such as this," Air Force Tech Sergeant Mark Stepaniak told Reuters from Guam.
The Air Force has an estimated 1,900 personnel on Guam while the Navy has 4,000 to 5,000.
The accident came at a time when emergency medical care is becoming a hot topic in the travel industry.
The U.S. State Department has issued warnings to travellers that some resort areas offer barely adequate or substandard medical care and emergency response facilities.
Travel industry experts point out that, due in large part to the lack of proper care for crash victims, vehicle accidents are the leading cause of death for tourists.
In the Guam accident, the emergency response was swift and substantial.

The U.S. Air Force sent about 90 people to the crash site, along with rescue and fire-fighting vehicles. They also set up a medical triage and treatment operation at the site in conjunction with a Navy field hospital.

The U.S. Navy deployed CH-46 Sea Knight helicopters to ferry at least 25 survivors to the U.S. Navy Hospital in Guam. In addition, Navy personnel used bulldozers to cut a path through grass more than 2.5 meters (eight feet) high, allowing emergency vehicles access to the crash site.
